reading.rtitle: How to run your slot -- the page we give every new director
paras: Your slot is twenty minutes and it is shorter than it sounds, because the last eight belong to the room. Plan on speaking for ten. In the opening, say what you want to cover and how many points there are, and then stop. We recommend saying the number out loud, because a room that knows there are three points waits for the third one instead of interrupting after the first.

Between the points, use a transition and make it a full sentence. That is the second point; the third one is different, and I want to spend longer on it. People avoid doing this because it feels mechanical, and then they wonder why nobody could follow them. A transition is not decoration. It is the only thing telling the room where you are.

When an objection comes, do not rush. Nobody expects you to answer in half a second, and starting to talk before you have decided what to say is how a good answer turns into a long one. Repeat the objection in your own words first: it buys you five seconds and it proves you understood. Then wrap up on time. Plan to finish two minutes early, decide who does what, and hand the follow-up to a name and a date. A meeting that ends without a name attached to something has not ended. It has just stopped.

listenings.text: Good morning. Today I am going to cover three points, and I plan to be finished in ten minutes so that we have time for questions. First, where the coverage numbers are. Second, what we decided about the discount and why. Third, and this is the one I want to spend longer on, what I need from this room before the fifteenth. So, the first point. Coverage is at nineteen per cent and we expected twenty-two. That is the second point finished. The third one is different, and it is the reason I asked for the slot. I need a decision today, not a conversation, and I will explain what I mean by that. Before I do, does anybody want me to clarify anything from the first two points? Good. Then let me finish and we will wrap up early.

People think running a meeting is about confidence, and it is mostly about structure. I have watched extremely confident people lose a room in four minutes because nobody could tell which point they were on. Three habits fix almost all of it. Say how many points there are, at the start. It sounds small and it changes everything, because a room that knows there are three will wait for the third instead of interrupting after the first. Second, make your transitions full sentences. Not just so, or moving on, but that is the second point and the third one is different. People avoid doing that because it feels mechanical, and then they wonder why nobody followed them. Third, and this is the one almost nobody does, plan to finish early. Not on time. Early. The two minutes you give back are the only part of the meeting anybody will thank you for.
